newsitem.title: USA: World Bank delays Croatia loan indefinitely.
newsitem.headline: World Bank delays Croatia loan indefinitely.

text.p: The World Bank postponed a decision on a planned $30 million loan to Croatia after a 90-minute debate on Tuesday when the United States said it was worried about Zagreb's commitment to peace accords.
U.S. State Department spokesman John Dinger told a news briefing the United States was concerned that Croatia had not complied in full with the 1995 Dayton agreement, which ended the Yugoslavia war.
"I understand there was broad multilateral support for that decision in view of Croatia's insufficient compliance with its obligations under the Dayton agreement," he said.

The World Bank confirmed that the loan had been postponed but would give no information on the discussions. Sources admitted it was unusual to delay a loan at the request of a member, even one as large and powerful as the United States.

The United States is the World Bank's biggest shareholder and has almost 15 percent of its voting power. But it would not by itself have had enough votes to block a decision on the planned Croatia loan or on other issues.

A U.S. Treasury official, who asked not to be named, said Washington was not alone in its objections to the release of the loan during a debate lasting 1-1/2 hours. "It was clear that a substantial number of major donors were not comfortable about making a decision to release the loan," he said.
The money would have been used to improve the banking system of Croatia, which recorded a respectable year-on-year inflation rate of 3.4 percent in June.

Peter Stek, the Dutch official who represents Croatia's interests at the World Bank, said Zagreb was bound to be disappointed at the World Bank decision. "Croatia, I am sure, is not overjoyed at the postponement, but given the situation I think the conclusion must be that postponement avoids the impression that might have arisen if there had been a vote."
Stek added: "This is a postponement, not a rejection."
U.S. concern had centred on worries that the Zagreb authorities were not doing enough to extradite suspected war criminals or allow the return of refugees from the fighting.
Dinger said Croatia's failure to meet its Dayton obligations could have wider implications.

"Failure to comply with one international agreement brings into question how it complies with other international agreements," he said. "For example, failing to comply with Dayton may have an implication on failing to comply with international financial institutions."
